c.tagline: Prayer flags, pine ridges, and the world's last Vajrayana capital.

taxi.fareNote: Government sets per-km rate cards (base fare plus ~25 Nu/km) but cabs rarely run meters in practice; confirm the fare with the driver, or agree a flat rate, before departing.

emergency.medical: 112 (ambulance); 110 for fire; 1010 general emergency access line
emergency.note: Bhutan has very low crime; the Royal Bhutan Police is helpful and English-speaking in Thimphu.

avoid.reason: Stray dog packs at night and occasional late-night drunken scuffles near downtown bars are the main annoyances.

hood_desc: The walkable commercial heart of Thimphu around Norzin Lam, packed with shops, cafes, the weekend market and the National Memorial Chorten; best for first-time visitors and anyone without a car.

A quieter mid-town corridor near Tashichho Dzong and the Chubachu circle, home to international-standard hotels; suits business travelers and those wanting comfort within easy walking distance of downtown.
A pine-forested residential ridge above the city near the Motithang Takin Preserve; ideal for couples, honeymooners and travelers wanting a calmer, scenic stay a short taxi ride from downtown.
A local, laid-back southern district along the Wang Chhu river near the Buddha Dordenma statue, with traditional guesthouses; good for budget travelers and longer stays seeking an authentic feel.
A no-frills area around the inter-city bus terminal with simple hotels and guesthouses; suits backpackers and those catching early buses to Paro, Punakha or Phuentsholing.

water.note: Water is often contaminated by the time it reaches the tap; drink bottled or boiled water only.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash on boarding; city routes charge a small flat/short-hop fare in ngultrum. Most visitors instead rely on hired cars with driver or taxis given the compact, hilly center and Bhutan's guided-tourism structure.
transit.hours: Roughly 7am-9pm on main routes; no late-night service, so taxis cover evenings and early mornings.
transit.note: Bhutan has no rail or metro; the small city bus network mainly serves residents, while tourists typically travel by private/hired vehicle.

bus: Bhutan Post City Bus Service (Thimphu urban routes)
Inter-city coaches from Thimphu's Changzamtog bus terminal to Paro, Punakha, Phuentsholing and beyond

airport.name: Paro International Airport (PBH)
airport.drive: 45-60 min via the Paro-Thimphu highway (only ~46 km but winding mountain road)

tip.r: Tipping isn't traditional but is increasingly appreciated for guides, drivers, and restaurant staff in tourist-oriented spots; 5-10% or a small flat amount is plenty.
